Text 2: The Extra Chair

When Kabir entered the art room, every group seemed complete. Four students were painting a city scene, while another group was building a cardboard tower. An empty chair stood near a quiet student named Tara, but the table was covered with carefully sorted paper strips.
"Is anyone sitting here?" Kabir asked.
Tara shook her head. "I am trying to weave a basket, but the strips keep slipping."
Kabir almost joined the city-painting group. Their bright poster looked exciting and nearly finished. Then he noticed Tara holding three loose strips with both hands. He pulled over the empty chair and said, "Perhaps one of us can hold while the other weaves."
Their first attempt collapsed. On the second, they clipped the base before weaving. By the end of the lesson, the basket was uneven but strong enough to hold six paintbrushes. Tara placed a small card beside it: "Designed by two patient problem-solvers." Kabir smiled. The unfinished basket suddenly seemed more interesting than the polished city scene.

Text 3: A Cooler Street

On sunny days, streets without shade can become much hotter than nearby parks. Trees cool a street in two ways. Their leaves block some sunlight, and water released from their leaves helps cool the surrounding air.
Planting any tree anywhere is not enough. A young tree needs space for roots, regular watering and protection from damage. Town planners must also choose species that suit the local climate. A tree planted directly beneath power lines may later require heavy cutting, while a tree with weak branches may be unsafe beside a busy path.
Some towns begin with a tree survey. They record where shade is missing, which trees are healthy and where underground pipes are located. This takes time, but it helps the town plant the right tree in the right place. The aim is not simply to count trees; it is to create shade that can last.

Text 2: The Silent Demonstration

Nisha had rehearsed every sentence for the science exhibition. Her model showed how a pulley could lift a heavy box with less effort. Just before the judges arrived, the string slipped out of its wheel.
"We should hide the model and explain it from the chart," whispered Joel.
Nisha looked at the loose string, then at the visitors waiting. Instead of beginning her memorised speech, she said, "Our machine has developed a problem. We will show you how we find it." They reset the string, tested the pulley and lifted the box. The judges asked fewer questions about the polished chart and more about the repair. Later, Nisha admitted that the broken demonstration had taught her more than the perfect rehearsals.

Text 3: Bringing Back a Coral Reef

Coral reefs support many sea creatures, but damaged reefs do not recover quickly. In some locations, scientists grow small coral pieces in underwater nurseries. When the pieces become larger, trained divers attach them to damaged parts of a reef.
This work can help, but it is not a complete solution. If water remains too warm or polluted, newly planted coral may die. Different coral species also respond differently to heat and disease. Scientists therefore monitor survival rates instead of assuming that every planted piece will succeed.
Local action matters as well. Reducing dirty water flowing from land, protecting fish that keep algae under control and limiting damage from anchors can improve the reef's chance of recovery. Coral planting is most useful when it is combined with action on the causes of damage.

Text 2: The Delayed Applause

Aarohi's violin solo ended, but the hall remained silent. For one uncomfortable second, she wondered whether she had missed the final note. Then she saw the conductor's raised hand. The last sound was still travelling through the hall, too soft to hear clearly but somehow present in the waiting faces.
The conductor lowered his hand. Applause broke out, louder than Aarohi expected. Backstage, her friend Sameer said, "That pause was dramatic. Did you plan it?"
Aarohi shook her head. "I thought something had gone wrong."
Later, the conductor explained that the quiet after a piece was part of listening. "An ending is not only the moment a musician stops," he said. "It is also the moment the audience realises what it has heard." On the bus home, Aarohi did not replay the applause in her mind. She remembered the silence before it.

Text 2: A Quiet Correction

The school magazine was due at the printer by noon when Leena noticed a sentence in the lead article: "The old auditorium will be demolished next month, the caretaker confirmed." She had recorded the interview herself. The caretaker had said the building might close for repairs; he had said nothing about demolition.
The article's writer, Varun, glanced at the clock. "It is one word. The headline is already designed. If we change it now, we miss the deadline."

Text 3: Low-Cost Air-Quality Sensors

Small air-quality sensors allow schools and residents to observe how particle levels change across streets and times of day. Because they are cheaper than reference-grade monitoring stations, many sensors can be installed. This wider coverage can reveal local patterns that a single station might miss.
Their readings, however, require care. Humidity can affect some sensors, and two devices placed side by side may report slightly different values. Researchers often compare, or calibrate, low-cost sensors against a reference instrument. They also examine trends over time rather than treating one unusual reading as a confirmed pollution event.
These sensors are therefore useful neither as toys nor as perfect replacements for official stations. Their strength lies in providing additional evidence when their limitations, maintenance and calibration are made clear.

Text 4: The Empty Platform

By the station clock, the last train had left seven minutes ago. Mira stood beneath the timetable and insisted that the clock was fast. It had always been fast, she told herself, although she could not remember ever checking it.
Across the tracks, a tea seller stacked metal cups. "No more trains tonight," he called.
Mira lifted her suitcase as if the train might appear in answer. Her brother's message - DON'T MISS IT AGAIN - glowed on her phone. She turned the screen face down.
A distant light trembled beyond the curve. For a moment she smiled. Then it rose above the tracks and separated into two headlights on the road behind the station. The tea seller did not look up.
Mira sat on the suitcase. "The timetable must be wrong," she said, but this time quietly, to no one who had asked.
